video_title: Richmond Fed’s Tom Barkin on the Surprisingly Resilient Real Economy | Odd Lots
gist: Recorded at Jackson Hole shortly after Kevin Warsh's hawkish speech, Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin gives on-the-ground color showing a consumer that is 'creatively' borrowing from the future to keep spending, a data-center construction boom straining electricians and equipment while crowding out other building, AI whose main current effect is political backlash and cautious hiring (not yet productivity), and a tariff story that has gone quiet because refund checks are now flowing to companies rather than costs flowing to consumers.

insights.claim: Barkin characterizes Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech as describing inflation moving in the wrong direction and current policy as 'not restrictive' — a combination that logically implies a case for rate hikes, even though Warsh stopped short of saying so explicitly.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: Markets should not assume a September cut is locked in; a hawkish leadership voice describing policy as not restrictive raises the tail risk of a pause or hike.
insights.quote: he said, okay, inflation seems to be going in the wrong direction right now. He described policy as not restrictive. So then you fill in the blanks and it's like, okay, that means rate hikes.

insights.claim: Barkin explicitly warns against reading Warsh's Jackson Hole speech as forward guidance for the September FOMC meeting, since Warsh himself is skeptical of forward guidance as a tool.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: Traders pricing September odds off the tone of the speech may be over-reading it; Barkin says the speaker's own framework argues against extracting a policy signal from it.
insights.quote: I don't think you should take any forward guidance from a speech from a guy who doesn't give forward guidance.

insights.claim: Barkin says the Fed is set to convene task forces that could revisit core elements of its communications strategy, up to and including whether it needs to publish specific dates or hold press conferences at all, given for most of the Fed's history the chair didn't hold press conferences.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: Expect a structural change to how the Fed communicates policy intentions under incoming leadership, which would affect how markets extract and price forward rate expectations.

insights.claim: Barkin personally criticizes the Fed's Summary of Economic Projections 'dot plot' as bad communication because the public and press often treat it as a Fed commitment (e.g., 'the Fed promised two more rate cuts') rather than as a scatter of independent, non-binding forecasts.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: Signals the dot plot's future prominence as a market-moving artifact may be reduced or reformatted; investors should be wary of over-weighting the median dot as a binding path.
insights.quote: if what comes out is I go do it, Chamber of Commerce in Greensboro. And somebody says to me, well, I see the fed promise two more rate rate cuts this year, then that's not good communication because that's not what we've done.

insights.claim: Countering Warsh's framing that inflation has been above target for 65 straight months (which Warsh called squarely on the Fed), Barkin offers an alternative reading: a 47-month period ending around March 2025 when inflation had fallen to 2.3-2.4% and the economy looked like it was 'landing,' followed by a fresh 18-month period in which new external shocks — AI-related demand, tariffs, and oil prices — pushed inflation back up.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: This '47+18 month' framing is likely to become the Fed's talking point to defend current policy against a hawkish 'the Fed is behind the curve' critique; it also flags AI capex, tariffs, and oil as the specific drivers behind the recent inflation re-acceleration.
insights.quote: you say, don't give me your excuses. It's been 65 months and it's been over. And, you know, maybe rates aren't that restrictive and maybe you have to think about it. And that's the argument I'm sure we're going to have.

themes.theme: Consumer Resilience Is Built on Hidden Borrowing, Not Just Wealth

insights.claim: Barkin's working theory for why consumers keep spending despite high prices and uncertainty is psychological: unlike the multi-year 'secular stagnation' that followed the Great Recession (job/home/savings losses), consumers emerged from Covid with elevated equity and home values plus leftover stimulus savings and adopted a 'bound and determined to spend' mindset that has persisted.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: This mindset-driven resilience argues consumer spending strength is more durable/psychological than purely wealth-driven, but also less rational — a regime that could reverse sharply once wealth gains or labor market conditions crack.
insights.quote: I think you had a mindset that just says, I'm bound and determined to spend.

insights.claim: Consumers are quietly funding continued spending by 'borrowing from the future' through under-the-radar channels: adult children moving back home and skipping rent, auto borrowers deliberately staying 60 days delinquent rather than paying (to avoid the 120-day repossession threshold), and consumers skipping summer gas bills because utilities are lenient in warm months but strict in winter — alongside a falling personal savings rate and a visible shift to private label and Walmart/Dollar stores.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: These are leading-indicator stress signals hidden beneath strong headline spending data; watch auto loan delinquency mix (60- vs 120-day) and utility payment/shutoff data heading into winter as an early warning before it shows up in retail sales.
insights.quote: I've talked to, auto lenders who talk about people being 60 days delinquent, not 120 days delinquent because they don't want to look... gas providers who say people aren't paying the gas bill during the summer because no one's going to have a problem with gas in the summer. It's the winter that matters.

insights.claim: Despite this credit-based, behavioral consumer resilience, the personal savings rate has declined but not collapsed — the pattern does not resemble panic-driven, buy-everything-now spending, suggesting the current strength is not yet a full-blown consumer distress signal.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Tempers a bearish 'consumer credit bubble' narrative — spending strength is coexisting with only a moderate savings decline rather than an outright debt binge, for now.

themes.theme: AI/Data-Center Buildout: Real Bottlenecks and a Possible Overbuild-to-Underbuild Swing

insights.claim: Barkin cites roughly $700 billion in data-center/AI-related construction announced in a single week at the start of February, which has produced acute, real shortages of switchgear, transformers, and electricians.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: A concrete bottleneck data point — watch electrical equipment suppliers (transformers, switchgear) and skilled-trades wage inflation as margin/timeline risk for the AI buildout.
insights.quote: 700 billion announced in one week, I think at the beginning of February alone. And for sure, if you're trying to find switch gears or transformers or electricians, they are very hot and in very short supply.

insights.claim: Construction activity is rotating across sectors rather than simply adding net capacity — office and multifamily starts are down sharply while industrial/data-center construction surges — and Barkin suspects the AI buildout may be crowding out competing construction, since multifamily developers cite rising construction costs, labor costs, and higher required equity (not just interest rates, which were similar in 2004-05 when building boomed) as the reason projects no longer 'pencil out.'
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: A structural under-supply may be forming in multifamily housing as capital, labor and materials get diverted to data centers — a medium-term bullish setup for rental prices and REITs exposed to housing scarcity.
insights.quote: you could argue that all this data center construction is making it more expensive to do this other construction, which means they're not doing this other construction because it's more expensive.

insights.claim: Barkin says the single biggest real-world effect of AI he's observed so far is political, not economic: every Chamber of Commerce meeting and town hall now generates questions about jobs, water use, and data centers.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: Local political/regulatory backlash (water use, zoning) is becoming a material constraint on data-center siting and buildout timelines — worth tracking as a supply-side risk to AI capex plans, alongside Austin Goolsbee's independent observation of the same complaints.
insights.quote: the number one impact is a political impact... every Chamber of Commerce meeting I do, every town hall, I do, I'm getting questions about jobs and water and data centers and all the rest of it.

insights.claim: Barkin explains the mechanism behind data-center political backlash: unlike a manufacturing plant, whose workers' kids play on local sports teams and create a community constituency, a data center brings tax revenue but very few permanent jobs, leaving no local workforce base to defend it politically.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: Explains why data-center tax-revenue pitches from economic developers often fail to win over residents — expect continued local resistance to new siting even as fiscal arguments favor these projects.
insights.quote: it brings tax dollars but doesn't bring enough workers... for the citizens to have friends who work in the data centers.

insights.claim: Barkin stresses genuine two-sided uncertainty in AI/data-center/energy footprint forecasting — the Fed and everyone else will 'get the numbers wrong,' and a political backlash could just as easily tip the buildout from overbuild into underbuild as it could continue driving overbuild.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: AI capex should be treated as a genuine swing factor for both growth and inflation with two-sided risk — not a one-way bet on the buildout continuing to accelerate indefinitely.
insights.quote: we're going to grow the AI footprint of this country massively, but we have no idea how massively... the one thing we know is we're going to get those numbers wrong.

themes.theme: AI's Actual Labor-Market Effect: Cautious Hiring, Not Yet Productivity

insights.claim: Barkin says AI is not yet delivering a broad productivity boom outside a few specific use cases (call-center agent substitution, programming, and heavy documentation/compliance work); the significant productivity gains businesses are currently realizing largely trace back to automation investments and new staffing/operating models adopted in 2021-22 during the post-pandemic labor shortage, not to generative AI itself.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the narrative that AI productivity gains are already visible in the data — current productivity should largely be attributed to prior labor-shortage-driven automation, implying AI capex has further to run before showing up in output data.
insights.quote: I don't think it's having this massive productivity impact quite yet outside of just a couple areas... the productivity boom we're seeing, which is significant, I think it's really been driven by [20]22 when you had people short workers.

insights.claim: The clearest current labor-market effect of AI is on hiring behavior: uncertain about the future, employers are choosing to try filling open roles with AI first before committing to a human hire, contributing to the broader 'low hire, low fire' labor market pattern.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: Helps explain soft-but-stable payroll growth; watch job openings and hiring-rate data as the leading indicator of whether AI substitution for new hires is broadening across industries.
insights.quote: why don't you leverage and see if you can't fill the job using AI first, and then we'll hire later that that's happening, you know, at some scale.

themes.theme: Inflation Regime Shift and a Housing Inflation Time Bomb

insights.claim: Barkin argues the disinflationary tailwinds of the 2010s — fracking-driven cheap energy, favorable demographics/labor supply, e-commerce, and globalization — are fading or reversing, making it plausible that the 'new normal' resembles today's more shock-prone, inflation-leaning environment rather than the prior decade, requiring the Fed to actively 'lean into the wind' rather than assume shocks are transitory.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: Supports a structurally higher, more shock-prone inflation regime thesis relevant to duration positioning, inflation-hedge allocation, and skepticism toward 'transitory shock' framing from the Fed.
insights.quote: I don't think it's ridiculous to imagine that ten years later, you might have a bunch of factors that would be bringing inflation up... I think that's the kind of risk we got. If you're in a world with an ever continuing set of inflationary shocks, you just have to lean against that wind.

insights.claim: Although soft housing construction and cooling rents are currently helping the Fed's inflation fight, Barkin thinks it's 'highly likely' that housing tightness returns as pent-up household-formation demand (families needing bigger homes) meets constrained inventory from today's weak building activity, pushing prices back up.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: Shelter/rent disinflation currently helping headline CPI may prove temporary — a bullish medium-term setup for homebuilders and rental-property owners and a risk to the Fed's inflation-cooling narrative.
insights.quote: at some point, you know, they'll have their second kid and they need a bigger house... And then if you don't have the housing inventory, you know, whether it's rental or, single family, then the prices will go back up.

themes.theme: Tariffs: Quiet Because Refunds Are Flowing, Pass-Through Is Uneven

insights.claim: Tariff discussion has gone quiet in Barkin's district largely because actual collections were always smaller than the headline announced numbers, and after a Supreme Court ruling, companies have spent the last 3-4 months receiving refunds rather than paying costs; those refunds are proving stimulative for earnings, but management commentary about 'reinvesting in the customer' via price cuts is mostly overstated — the money is going more toward marketing, store refits, and staffing than lower prices.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: Tariff refunds are an underappreciated, modest earnings tailwind for affected companies in the near term, but investors should not expect them to translate into meaningful consumer price relief.
insights.quote: when you collect your you're not talking about it quite as much... They're very positive for earnings. If you read through the earnings reports of the people who've gotten the refunds, you hear, they're going to reinvest it in the customer... I think it's a lot more marketing store refits, you know, staffing levels.

insights.claim: Tariff cost pass-through is sharply bifurcated: B2B companies report they have successfully passed through nearly all tariff costs to customers, while B2C companies — especially those selling through big-box retailers to low-to-moderate income shoppers — are struggling to raise prices because those retailers actively resist increases, instead absorbing the cost through productivity gains and minimal wage pressure.
insights.speaker: Tom Barkin
insights.so_what: Big-box retailers are absorbing tariff costs via productivity rather than passing them to consumers, meaning tariff-driven inflation will show up more in supplier/B2C margins than in headline goods prices at mass retail — a margin risk to watch in suppliers selling into big-box channels rather than in consumer price data.
insights.quote: The B2B companies I talked to to a person they're convinced they're passing it through... those people who sell into the major big box retailers, they tell me they're having a devil of a time trying to pass it through... those big box retailers, they're truly our strongest soldiers in the fight against inflation.
